seo.title: 27 Emblem and Badge Logos Explained
seo.description: 27 famous emblem and badge logos explained by a brand designer: seals, shields, crests and labels from Harley-Davidson, NASA and Ford to Porsche, LEGO and IKEA.

intro:
An emblem logo puts the brand name inside a shape: a seal, a shield, a crest or a badge. The name and the symbol are locked together, so you always see them as one piece. Think of the Harley-Davidson bar and shield, the NASA meatball or the blue Ford oval.

Logo design quick course: this guide is part of my series on logo types. Read the others on script logos, mascot logos, monogram logos, wordmark logos, lettermark logos, abstract logos, symmetry and negative space, or start with the overview of all types of logos.

What is an emblem logo?

An emblem is a logo where the text sits inside a symbol or frame instead of next to it. That is the difference from a combination mark. Nike can use the swoosh with or without its name, but you can't pull the words out of the Harley-Davidson shield without breaking the logo.

A badge logo is the same idea, used on products: patches, labels, bottle caps and stickers. Converse's ankle patch, the Levi's batwing and the Jack Daniel's label are all badges. In this guide I use both words, because the design rules are the same.

Where emblems come from

Emblems are the oldest kind of logo. Long before brands, kings, cities, guilds and churches used seals, coats of arms and crests to sign documents and mark property. A wax seal pressed into a letter was an emblem: a picture and a name in one small, official shape.

The Great Seal of the United States, adopted by Congress in 1782, follows the same rules: a shield, a motto on a banner and stars, all inside one circle. Universities, sports clubs and car makers later borrowed this language. That is why Harvard, FC Barcelona and Porsche still look like coats of arms, and why emblems feel official, traditional and trustworthy.

Three types of emblem logos

Round emblems: seals, roundels and ovals, like Ford, NASA and BMW. A circle feels complete and works well on wheels, caps and app icons.

Shields and crests: Harley-Davidson, the NFL, Porsche and FC Barcelona. Shields come from armour and heraldry, so they suggest strength, protection and belonging.

Labels, patches and badges: Jack Daniel's, Levi's, LEGO and IKEA. These are rectangles and tags that look like product labels, because that is where they started.

The problem with emblems: small sizes

An emblem packs a lot into a small space, so it is the first logo type to break when it shrinks. Fine lines, small type and decorative details fill in on a bottle cap and turn to mush on an app icon. Simple badges like LEGO's red square still read at any size.

That is why many brands have simplified their emblems. Starbucks dropped the ring with its name in 2011 and kept only the siren. BMW flattened its roundel in 2020, Nissan switched to a thin outline badge the same year, and Warner Bros. redrew its shield in 2019. When I design an emblem, I always design a small version too: a simplified mark or monogram for favicons, social profiles and embroidery.

Below are 27 famous emblem and badge logos, American brands first and then the rest of the world, across cars, food, sport, fashion, finance and more. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation.

logoResearch.name: Ford
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ford was founded in Detroit in 1903, and the blue oval first appeared on a car on the 1927 Model A.
observations: A white script name sits inside a deep blue oval.
The script feels personal and traditional, like a signature on a classic car.

logoResearch.name: NASA
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The NASA insignia, nicknamed the meatball, was designed by James Modarelli in 1959.
observations: White letters sit on a blue sphere scattered with stars.
A red wing-shaped swoosh cuts across the circle and stands for flight.

logoResearch.name: Burger King
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Burger King's 2021 rebrand brought back a bun-shaped logo close to the one it used from 1969 to 1999.
observations: The name is sandwiched between two halves of a bun.
Round, chunky letters make the logo look as tasty as the food.

logoResearch.name: Hard Rock Cafe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Americans Isaac Tigrett and Peter Morton opened the first Hard Rock Cafe in London in 1971.
observations: A heavy brush script sits over a yellow circle with CAFE inside.
The circle turns the name into a badge that sells on millions of T-shirts.

logoResearch.name: Gulf
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gulf Oil was founded in Pittsburgh in 1901, and its orange disc became famous on Le Mans racing cars.
observations: The name sits on a blue band across an orange disc.
Orange and light blue are so linked to racing that the colours alone say Gulf.

logoResearch.name: BMW
logoResearch.verifiedFact: BMW introduced a flat, transparent version of its roundel in 2020; the blue and white come from the colours of Bavaria.
observations: The letters BMW sit on the outer ring around the blue and white quarters.
The circular emblem shows how company history can be preserved in a logo.

logoResearch.name: Nissan
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Nissan unveiled its flat, thin-line badge in 2020, the first big redesign in about 20 years.
observations: The name runs straight through an open ring.
Thin lines make the badge light enough to glow on the front of an electric car.

logoResearch.name: Nivea
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Beiersdorf introduced the blue and white Nivea tin in 1925.
observations: White capitals sit in the middle of a deep blue circle.
The logo is the lid of the famous tin, so the product and the brand look the same.

logoResearch.name: Chupa Chups
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Enric Bernat founded Chupa Chups in Spain in 1958, and Salvador Dalí designed its logo in 1969.
observations: A red script sits inside a yellow daisy.
Dalí placed the logo on top of the wrapper so it is always visible.

logoResearch.name: Harley-Davidson
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Harley-Davidson was founded in Milwaukee in 1903 and first used the bar and shield in 1910.
observations: The name sits on a black bar across an orange and black shield.
The badge is bold enough for tattoos, fuel tanks and leather jackets.

logoResearch.name: NFL
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The NFL was founded in 1920, and its shield was redrawn in 2008 with eight stars and a football on top.
observations: Heavy red letters fill a blue and white shield.
The shield looks like a badge of honour, which suits a league built on tradition.

logoResearch.name: Warner Bros.
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Warner Bros. was founded in 1923 by four brothers, and Pentagram redrew the WB shield in 2019.
observations: The WB letters sit inside a shield.
The shield has been redrawn many times, but its shape is instantly recognisable on film.

logoResearch.name: UPS
logoResearch.verifiedFact: UPS was founded in Seattle in 1907; Paul Rand drew its shield with a tied parcel in 1961, and the parcel was removed in 2003.
observations: Lowercase ups letters sit inside a brown shield.
A gold outline and a curved top make the shield feel modern rather than military.

logoResearch.name: Harvard
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Harvard was founded in 1636, and its motto, Veritas, appears on three open books in the shield.
observations: The letters VE RI TAS are spread across three books on a crimson shield.
The laurel wreath and banner turn the shield into a formal academic seal.

logoResearch.name: Porsche
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Porsche crest, introduced in 1952, combines the horse of Stuttgart with the colours and antlers of Württemberg.
observations: A black horse sits in the centre of a gold shield.
Red stripes and antlers around it tell the story of the company's home region.

logoResearch.name: Lamborghini
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ferruccio Lamborghini founded the car maker in 1963; the bull reflects his zodiac sign, Taurus.
observations: A charging bull sits inside a gold-edged black shield.
The bull suggests power and aggression, which suits supercars.

logoResearch.name: FC Barcelona
logoResearch.verifiedFact: FC Barcelona was founded by Joan Gamper in 1899.
observations: The FCB initials run across a band in the middle of the crest.
The cross of Saint George, the Catalan flag and the club's blue and red stripes share one shape.

logoResearch.name: TAG Heuer
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Edouard Heuer founded the watch company in Switzerland in 1860, and TAG bought it in 1985.
observations: Green and red panels sit inside a pointed shield.
The two colours keep the names of the two companies apart.

logoResearch.name: Jack Daniel's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Jack Daniel's distillery in Lynchburg, Tennessee, says it was registered in 1866.
observations: The name arches over an ornate Old No. 7 oval on a black label.
The logo is the bottle label, so it looks the same on a shelf and a T-shirt.

logoResearch.name: Converse
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Converse was founded in Massachusetts in 1908, and Chuck Taylor's signature was added to the ankle patch in 1932.
observations: A red star sits in the middle of a round patch, with the brand name on the ring.
The script signature makes the badge feel personal, like an autograph.

logoResearch.name: Levi's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Levi Strauss & Co. was founded in San Francisco in 1853, and the batwing logo was created in 1967.
observations: White letters sit on a red batwing shape.
The batwing's curved bottom echoes the stitching on the back pocket of Levi's jeans.

logoResearch.name: Patagonia
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Yvon Chouinard founded Patagonia in Ventura, California, in 1973.
observations: The skyline of Monte Fitz Roy sits against stripes of a sunset sky.
The label works like a postcard of the brand's world: mountains and the outdoors.

logoResearch.name: Wells Fargo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Henry Wells and William Fargo founded Wells Fargo in 1852 to serve the California Gold Rush.
observations: Gold serif capitals are stacked inside a solid red square.
The box works as a sign, an app icon and a stamp without any changes.

logoResearch.name: Ray-Ban
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bausch & Lomb launched Ray-Ban in 1937 to make sunglasses for American pilots.
observations: A white handwritten script sits inside a red rectangle.
The script looks like it was signed on the spot, which suits a fashion brand.

logoResearch.name: Stella Artois
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Stella Artois traces its brewing history to the Den Hoorn brewery in Leuven, founded in 1366.
observations: An ornate emblem with a red banner looks like an old beer label.
The heritage details signal tradition and quality.

logoResearch.name: LEGO
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ole Kirk Christiansen founded LEGO in Billund, Denmark, in 1932; the name comes from leg godt, play well.
observations: White, bubbly letters with black and yellow outlines sit in a red square.
The outlines make the letters look like toys, as soft and solid as the bricks.

logoResearch.name: IKEA
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in Sweden in 1943; the name combines his initials with his farm and village.
observations: Blue capitals sit in a yellow oval inside a blue rectangle.
The blue and yellow come from the Swedish flag.

listIntro: The boards below show all 27 emblem and badge logos in one consistent format, grouped into round emblems, shields and crests, and labels and badges.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the size or success of the company behind it.
sectionNames: Round emblems: seals, roundels and ovals
sectionIntroductions: Circles, ovals and roundels are the friendliest emblems. The name either wraps around a ring, like BMW, or runs straight through the middle, like Nissan, Nivea and Gulf.
Shields and crests borrow from heraldry and armour. They signal strength, tradition and belonging, which is why car makers, sports leagues and universities love them.
Labels, patches and boxes started on products: bottles, jeans, sneakers and toys. They work like a stamp, so the logo looks the same on the shelf and on a T-shirt.
sectionBridge: This is a visual study of emblem logos, not a ranking of companies.
Look at how each emblem fits the name inside one shape and how much detail it can carry before it stops reading.
entryFallbacks: The emblem locks the name and the symbol into one shape.
Notice how the logo would look on a sign, a patch and an app icon.

findings.heading: The shape tells the story
findings.text: Circles feel friendly and complete, shields feel strong and official, and labels feel like products.

findings.heading: Heritage is the point
findings.text: Porsche, Harvard, Stella Artois and Jack Daniel's use emblems to show history and tradition.

findings.heading: Emblems sell merchandise
findings.text: Harley-Davidson, NASA, Hard Rock Cafe and the NFL earn money from patches, caps and T-shirts.

findings.heading: Simple badges survive
findings.text: LEGO, IKEA, Wells Fargo and Nivea use one bold shape and one name, so they read at any size.

findings.heading: Flat is the new standard
findings.text: BMW, Nissan, Burger King and Warner Bros. have simplified their emblems to work on screens.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for an emblem logo
checklistItems: Is the name easy to read inside the shape?
Does it still work at 24 pixels and in one colour?
Is there one clear symbol, not five?
Can it be embroidered, engraved or printed on a cap?
Do you have a simplified small version for icons and social media?
logoRosterConfig.conclusionHtml:
How to design an emblem logo

1. Pick a shape. A circle feels friendly and complete, a shield feels strong and official, and a rectangle feels like a label. Choose the shape that fits your story and where the logo will live.

2. Fit the name. Set the name inside the shape first, before any decoration. Use a bold, simple typeface, and curve it along a ring only if it stays easy to read.

3. Add one symbol. One clear idea is enough: Porsche's horse, Lamborghini's bull or Converse's star. More details make the emblem harder to remember and to reproduce.

4. Make a small mark. Test the emblem at 24 pixels, in one colour and as embroidery. If it breaks, design a simplified version for small sizes, like Starbucks did with its siren.

Want an emblem that lasts?

A great emblem logo feels like a badge people want to wear. It tells a story with one shape, one name and one symbol, and it has a simpler version for small sizes. Harley-Davidson, NASA and LEGO prove that the best emblems can last for decades.

faq.question: What is an emblem logo?
faq.answer: An emblem logo places the brand name inside a symbol or frame, like a seal, shield, crest or badge. The text and the shape are locked together, as in the Harley-Davidson bar and shield, the NASA meatball and the Ford oval.

faq.question: What is the difference between an emblem and a badge logo?
faq.answer: They are the same type of logo. Badge logo usually describes an emblem used on products, like a patch, label or bottle cap, such as Converse's ankle patch or the Levi's batwing.

faq.question: What is the difference between an emblem and a combination mark?
faq.answer: In a combination mark the symbol and the name sit side by side and can be used separately, like Nike's swoosh and wordmark. In an emblem the name sits inside the symbol, so they always appear together.

faq.question: Are emblem logos good for small businesses?
faq.answer: Yes, if heritage, trust or merchandise matter to you, like breweries, coffee shops, schools, sports clubs and outdoor brands. Keep the design simple and ask for a small simplified version for icons and social media.

faq.question: How much does an emblem logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity, including the emblem and its small version, in one week for a flat $3,000.
